title: Finite map to the affine line
statement:
Let $C_0$ be a smooth affine curve which is geometrically a connected
curve. There is a smooth curve $C'_0$, geometrically a connected curve, containing $C_0$ as a
dense open with finite complement, and a finite generically etale
morphism $g:C'_0\to\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$.

proof.text: Use the finite-field convention $k_0=\mathbf F_q$, of characteristic $p>0$, from [def-weil-finite-field-fiber]. The geometric connected curve hypothesis includes nonemptiness and dimension one. Smoothness gives normality by [lem-sc-smooth-normal]. Apply [lem-wf-curve-normal-smooth-compactification] to obtain a smooth projective geometrically connected curve $\overline C_0$ containing $C_0$ as a dense open, with reduced boundary $D_0$ finite over $k_0$. These are normal connected Noetherian curves and hence integral: finite type over a field is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian], and distinct irreducible components cannot meet in a local domain, so [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finite-components] supplies finitely many components, which are disjoint open and closed subsets. The same argument after algebraic closure shows that $\overline C_0$ is geometrically integral.

source.place: Proof, first sentence: smooth projective completion; replace the algebraically-closed-only compactification citation by the existing finite-field version.

proof.text: The boundary $D_0$ is nonempty. Otherwise $C_0=\overline C_0$ would be both affine and proper over $k_0$, so [lem-sc-proper-affine-finite-general] would make it finite over $k_0$. Such a scheme has dimension zero: a prime quotient of a finite-dimensional $k_0$-algebra is a finite-dimensional domain, where multiplication by a nonzero element is injective and therefore surjective, so it is a field. This contradicts dimension one. Choose a closed point $s\in D_0$ and put $d_s=[\kappa(s):k_0]>0$. This degree is finite since $D_0$ is finite over $k_0$. The residue field is a finite field of order $q^{d_s}$: each of its elements is a root of $T^{q^{d_s}}-T$, whose derivative is $-1$, so the residue extension is separable.

source.place: Proof, first paragraph: existence of a boundary point and its residue degree. The finite-dimensional-domain argument is elementary.

proof.text: By [lem-sc-point-cartier], the reduced point $s$ is an effective Cartier divisor. If $\mathcal I_s$ is its invertible ideal, set $\mathcal L_n=(\mathcal I_s^\vee)^{\otimes n}=\mathcal O_{\overline C_0}(ns)$ for $n\geq0$. Use the function field (the stalk at the generic point) and its affine fraction-field interpretation from [def-sc-function-field]. Concretely, these line bundles are subsheaves of the rational functions, regular away from $s$; at $s$, for a local equation $t$ of $s$, they are $t^{-n}\mathcal O_{\overline C_0,s}$. This description follows directly by dualizing the local invertible ideal $(t)$ and tensoring. Write $g=\dim_{k_0}H^1(\overline C_0,\mathcal O_{\overline C_0})$. Choose $m\geq1$ with $p\nmid m$ and $(m-1)d_s>2g-2$; the integers $1+rp$ are unbounded. The general-field Riemann–Roch theorem [sk-thm-picard-rr] gives $h^0(\mathcal L_m)=m d_s+1-g$ and $h^0(\mathcal L_{m-1})=(m-1)d_s+1-g$. Thus their difference is $d_s>0$.

source.place: Proof, first paragraph: Cartier point, choice of m and Riemann–Roch dimension jump; use the existing general-field theorem, including its residue-degree convention.

proof.text: Choose $f\in H^0(\overline C_0,\mathcal L_m)$ outside $H^0(\overline C_0,\mathcal L_{m-1})$. The local description in Step 3 shows that $f$ is regular away from $s$ and has a pole of exactly order $m$ at $s$: failing to lie in $\mathcal L_{m-1}$ can occur only at $s$, and $f\in t^{-m}A\setminus t^{-m+1}A$, for $A=\mathcal O_{\overline C_0,s}$. In particular $t^m f$ is a unit. The sections $1,f$ generate $\mathcal L_m$: away from $s$, $1$ generates it, and at $s$ the section $f$ generates it. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-sections-morphism-to-proj-polynomial-ring] with $A=k_0$, two homogeneous coordinates, $s_0=1$, $s_1=f$, to obtain $h:\overline C_0\to\mathbf P^1_{k_0}$. On $D_+(x_0)$ its coordinate $x_1/x_0$ pulls back to $f$; near $s$ the coordinate $x_0/x_1$ pulls back to $1/f$. Its inverse image of infinity has underlying set exactly $\{s\}$.

source.place: Proof, second paragraph: the base-point-free pair 1,f and its projective morphism, with the inverse image of infinity.

proof.text: The projective line is proper, hence separated over $k_0$, by [lemma-nagata-projective-space-base-change-proper]. Since $\overline C_0$ is proper over $k_0$, [lem-weil-pbc-proper-over-separated] makes $h$ proper. It is nonconstant: $s$ maps to infinity, whereas the nonempty open $\overline C_0\setminus\{s\}$ maps to the affine chart. For any closed point $y\in\mathbf P^1$, the fibre is a proper closed subset of the integral dimension-one curve $\overline C_0$, hence has dimension at most zero; [lem-sc-dim0-finite] makes its underlying set finite. Every nongeneric point of $\overline C_0$ is closed, and properness sends it to a closed point, so the fibre over the generic point of $\mathbf P^1$ contains at most the generic point of $\overline C_0$. Thus all fibres are finite. The target is locally Noetherian (its two standard charts are spectra of the PID $k_0[T]$). Apply [thm-pqf-finite-iff-proper-finite-fibres] to conclude that $h$ is finite.

source.place: Proof, second paragraph: properness, finite fibres, and the finite-morphism criterion. This expands the omitted finite-fibre argument.

proof.text:
Apply [lem-a1-uniformizer-differential-basis] at the closed point $s$ of $\overline C_0$. Its residue field is finite over $k_0$ and separable, so $A=\mathcal O_{\overline C_0,s}$ is a DVR, with uniformizer $t$ and $\Omega_{A/k_0}=A\,dt$. In the coordinate $z=x_0/x_1$ at infinity, $h^\sharp z=1/f=t^m v$ for a unit $v\in A$. Write $dv=a\,dt$, $a\in A$. The derivation rules give
$$d(h^\sharp z)=t^{m-1}(m v+t a)\,dt
eq0.$$
Indeed $m v+t a$ has nonzero reduction modulo $(t)$ because $p
mid m$ and $v$ is a unit; it is therefore a unit of $A$, and $t^{m-1}
eq0$ in the domain $A$. Thus $dh$ is nonzero. This local calculation proves the nonvanishing used by the blueprint without assuming that $s$ is rational.

source.place: Proof, third paragraph: prime-to-p pole order forces nonzero differential; expanded using Stacks Tag 0C1E and the Leibniz rule.

proof.text: Both $\overline C_0$ and $\mathbf P^1_{k_0}$ are smooth integral curves. For the latter, the two standard charts are $\operatorname{Spec}k_0[T]$: this algebra is finitely presented, and lifting a map across a first-order thickening amounts to choosing a lift of the single element which is the image of $T$, verifying smoothness directly from [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. The differential criterion [lem-a1-nonzero-differential-generically-etale] applied to the nonzero $dh$ provides a nonempty open $V\subseteq\overline C_0$ on which $h$ is étale. Hence $h$ is generically étale.

source.place: Proof, third paragraph: nonzero differential implies generic etaleness; Stacks Tag 0C1C.

proof.text: Set $C'_0=\overline C_0\setminus\{s\}$. By Step 4 this is exactly $h^{-1}(\mathbf A^1_{k_0})$, so $g=h|_{C'_0}:C'_0\to\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$ is the base change of the finite map $h$ along the standard open immersion. It is finite by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-morphism-permanence](a). The nonempty opens $V$ and $C'_0$ intersect in the integral curve $\overline C_0$, and $g$ is étale there by restriction, hence generically étale. Smoothness and etaleness restrict to opens because their affine-local presentations and stalk maps are unchanged [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-etale-morphism]. Thus the open $C'_0$ is smooth, and its geometric base change is a nonempty open of the smooth geometrically integral $\overline C_0$, hence integral and connected. It contains $C_0$ because $s$ is in its boundary; the inclusion is dense and its complement is the finite set $D_0\setminus\{s\}$. These are all the required assertions.

source.place: Proof, final sentences: restrict over the affine chart, use the actual finite-base-change node, and check the open enlargement and geometric connectedness.

proof_origin.place: Proof, all three paragraphs, repaired citations and expanded local differential calculation; auxiliary statements from Stacks Tags 0C1C and 0C1E.

split_report.blueprint: Steps 1–3 realize paragraph 1 (completion, boundary, Cartier point and dimension jump); Steps 4–5 realize paragraph 2 (1,f and finiteness); Steps 6–8 realize paragraph 3 (nonzero differential, generic etaleness and affine restriction).

tool_uses.why: Normality of a smooth curve over a field is a generic geometry tool needed to apply the finite-field completion; the unit supplies no separate normality result.

Use the existing finite-field compactification rather than the algebraically-closed-only compactification mistakenly cited in the item. It supplies the same completion step and does not replace the unit route.
The generic local fact that a closed point of a smooth curve is Cartier supplies the pole line bundle.
The existing general-field Riemann–Roch theorem supplies the exact h0 formulas with residue degrees; the narrower imported lem-sc-riemann-roch is insufficient over k0.
The general construction of a map to projective space from generating sections supplies h and its chart formulas; it is a tool, not an alternate curve argument.
Properness of projective space is used only to get separatedness of the target in the standard proper-source argument.
Finiteness of a zero-dimensional closed subset over a field is the finite-fibre tool.
The generic proper-plus-finite-fibres criterion is exactly the finiteness step already present in the blueprint.
Finiteness of the irreducible components of a Noetherian scheme is the generic topological tool in the normal connected implies integral argument.
